core: Beat as a regularly recurring musical pulse
Listening for a beat and distinguishing a beat from individual musical events
The relationship of beat to rhythm, meter, tempo, and accent
supporting: Beat units in common Western notation
How a steady pulse can support ensemble coordination and listener expectation
Careful descriptions when a recording does not make a stable pulse clear
outOfScope: Detailed time-signature instruction and conducting patterns
A claim that all music has a steady or equally spaced beat
Performance prescriptions or advanced rhythmic transcription

claims.claim: A beat is a pulse in music that regularly recurs and can often be tapped or clapped along with.
Rhythm concerns the organization of musical events in time, while beat is the recurring pulse that may provide a reference for that organization.
Meter groups beats into recurring patterns; in simple meter, a time signature communicates both beats per measure and the beat unit in Western notation.
Tempo is the rate at which beats pass, so changing tempo does not by itself change the underlying beat grouping.
A music passage can weaken, disrupt, or omit an easily perceived steady pulse; an absence of an obvious pulse should not be treated as an absence of musical time or rhythm.
Accents may help listeners hear a hierarchy among beats, but louder sound and structural strength are not interchangeable in every performance context.
